content: The mental status of one patient has improved significantly, and this individual no longer requires ventilatory support. Another patient, who underwent a liver transplantation, experienced fever, cough, and malaise seven days post-transplantation. However, there was no clinical evidence of encephalitis in this patient. These symptoms resolved, and the patient was subsequently discharged from the hospital. Laboratory testing of the patient’s serum for West Nile Virus (WNV) is currently underway. To date, WNV infection in organ transplant recipients has not been previously reported, and the risk of WNV transmission through donated organs remains unknown. Among the four organ recipients, three developed encephalitis. Typically, only one in 150 WNV infections progresses to encephalitis or meningitis. It is unclear whether immunosuppressed individuals, such as organ transplant recipients, are at an increased risk of severe WNV-related disease following infection. Similarly, it is unknown if the mode of transmission contributed to the higher risk of encephalitis in these organ transplant recipients. The organ donor may have acquired the WNV infection either through a mosquito bite or via blood products received after sustaining a fatal injury. Based on preliminary findings from this investigation, clinicians should remain vigilant for the possibility of WNV infection in organ transplant recipients and patients receiving blood transfusions. Rapid diagnostic testing for WNV is available through state and local health departments for clinicians who suspect WNV infection. Public health officials have implemented precautionary measures, including the withdrawal and testing of any remaining blood products from donors whose blood was provided to the organ donor. Blood donors whose products were given to the organ donor, as well as other recipients of blood from these donors, are being contacted for WNV testing. This represents the first reported case of potential WNV transmission via organ transplantation. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to justify changes to organ or blood donor screening and testing protocols or to the clinical use of donated organs and blood. During the reporting period from August 29 to September 4, a total of 257 laboratory-confirmed human cases of WNV-associated illness were reported across multiple states, including Illinois (94 cases), Louisiana (34 cases), Ohio (16 cases), Tennessee (15 cases), Michigan (14 cases), Mississippi (13 cases), Missouri (12 cases), New York (8 cases), Kentucky (7 cases), Alabama (5 cases), Texas (5 cases), Indiana (4 cases), North Dakota (4 cases), South Dakota (4 cases), Wisconsin (4 cases), Arkansas (3 cases), Minnesota (3 cases), Nebraska (3 cases), Virginia (2 cases), Connecticut (1 case), Florida (1 case), Iowa (1 case), Maryland (1 case), Massachusetts (1 case), Pennsylvania (1 case), and South Carolina (1 case). During this period, Arkansas, Connecticut, Iowa, Minnesota, North Dakota, Pennsylvania, and South Carolina reported their first human cases of WNV for 2002. Additionally, during the same reporting period, WNV infections were identified in 653 dead crows, 360 other dead birds, 322 horses, and 456 mosquito pools. For the year 2002, a total of 737 human cases with laboratory evidence of recent WNV infection have been reported from various states, including Louisiana (205 cases), Illinois (165 cases), Mississippi (104 cases), Texas (43 cases), Ohio (40 cases), Missouri (37 cases), Michigan (29 cases), Tennessee (19 cases), Alabama (13 cases), New York (13 cases), Indiana (10 cases), Kentucky (10 cases), South Dakota (7 cases), Georgia (6 cases), Wisconsin (6 cases), Nebraska (4 cases), North Dakota (4 cases), Arkansas (3 cases), Minnesota (3 cases), Virginia (3 cases), Florida (2 cases), Maryland (2 cases), Massachusetts (2 cases), Oklahoma (2 cases), Connecticut (1 case), the District of Columbia (1 case), Iowa (1 case), Pennsylvania (1 case), and South Carolina (1 case). Among patients with available data, the median age was 52 years (range: 9 months to 98 years), and 57% (341 cases) were male. Illness onset dates ranged from June 10 to August 28. A total of 35 human deaths have been reported, with a median age of 76 years (range: 48 to 94 years). Of these deaths, 57% (20 cases) occurred in men. In addition, 3,243 dead crows and 2,232 other dead birds with WNV infection have been reported from 39 states, New York City, and the District of Columbia. A total of 1,159 WNV infections in mammals (all but one in horses) have been reported from 27 states, including Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Virginia, and Wyoming.
